text: Hi, I am Sefika presenting this work together
with Jana Hofmann from Senckenberg.
In this presentation, we look at how
biodiversity collection data, specifically type specimen
catalogs, can be made more suitable for AI and
ML workflows.
Our focus is on combining established biodiversity standards
with ML Commons Croissant and metadata format
designed for
ML ready datasets. Broader questions behind this
work is
how can we make valuable historical
biodiversity data not only FAIR but also easier for modern
AI systems to discover, understand, and reuse?
I will introduce why biodiversity data matter for AI
connect with
FAIR principles and Croissant, and present our
workflows from historical catalogs to AI-ready dataset.
I will then show the
Croissant and Darwin Core mapping, FAIR
evaluation impact, and key takeaways.
Biodiversity data are increasingly being used
in AI applications. Examples include
species identification, named entity recognition, taxonomic knowledge
extraction, and building
biodiversity knowledge graphs. However, historical collection
catalogs create several challenges.
Much of their information is stored as unstructured or
semi-structured text. Human specialists may be able to read
records, but they often lack the explicit
machine-readable metadata that computational
workflows need.
As a result, valuable collection information can be difficult
to reuse directly for AI and ML. This
motivates a workflow that transforms historical
catalog content into structured, standardized, and
machine-readable data while preserving the biodiversity semantics.
The FAIR principles, findable,
accessible,
interoperable, and reusable, provide an important
foundation for AI-ready data. For ML, FAIRness
is not only about making a dataset available,
it makes experiments more reproducible, improves data
clarity and quality, makes the dataset easier to share,
and
can support more reliable model development.
In this work, we treat FAIR principles and AI readiness as
closely connected. A dataset that has a
well-described structure, semantics prevalence, and access
information is
much easier for both people and
computational systems to reuse. The goal is therefore
not to replace the FAIR principles, but to extend their
practical
values into
AI and ML workflows.
This brings us to ML Commons
Croissant, introduced as the metadata format for
ML-ready datasets.
Croissant provides a standardized, machine-readable
way to describe the dataset. It represents the data
structure and resources in a form ML tools can
interpret, rather than relying only on human-readable
documentation.
An important advantage is platform workflow
integration. Croissant supports the dataset use in
AI ecosystem, including platforms such as Hugging Face machine
learning pipelines. For our use case, the key benefits
are standardization across systems, easier
workflow integration, and clearer path from
biodiverse data to dataset usable for
model training.
This slide emphasizes Croissant as a common metadata
layer connecting three groups. First, data creators can
describe the dataset structure, resources, and semantics using
standardized ML-readable metadata.
Second, data repositories can publish
that metadata alongside the dataset, improving
consistent discovery across ML-oriented
platforms such as Hugging Face, Kaggle, OpenML.
Third, data users can search, understand, and load the dataset
more directly into the ML
workflows and frameworks. The key message is create
once, publish anywhere, and use everywhere.
For biodiverse collections, this common metadata layer can
help connect domain-specific data standard with the wider
ML ecosystem.
Here is the proposed workflow. We start with type specimen
catalog. A catalog record may contain specifically
rich information, but much of it appears as unstructured
historical text. In the next step, LLMs, for
example, GPT and Qwen, can be used to extract
structured information from that text.
The extracted information is then represented using
the Darwin Core metadata so that biodiversity concepts
follow an established community standard.
After that, Croissant metadata describes the resulting
dataset in a machine-readable form suitable for
ML workflows. So the transformation is type specimen
catalog, unstructured text, LLM assistant extraction,
Darwin Core metadata, and then Croissant
metadata.
Intended output is an AI-ready dataset.
A central
part of the approach is mapping Darwin Core elements into a
Croissant representation. For example, scientific name
can become a field that provides a special label for
ML classification. Genus can be
represented as a taxonomic feature, and
individual count as an integer-valued quantity feature.
The catalog number is particularly important because it serves
as a unique specimen or record
identifier. Locality provides a geographic feature.
Event date provides temporal metadata.
Collector captures the collection prevalence and type status
to present the type specimen classification.
The point is not to discard the Darwin Core.
Instead, it preserves its biodiverse semantics and
expresses those elements with a metadata structure that
ML systems can understand.
The overall goal shown at the bottom of the slide is
to bridge the biodiverse standards with AI metadata
standards.
This slide shows how Darwin Core records are represented
in Croissant using
ML-readable JSON-LD. Each
specimen attribute becomes an explicit field with a
defined data type, making biodiverse data easier to
discover, integrate, and use directly in ML
workflows.
We also evaluate the dataset's FAIRness.
The pipeline measures the FAIR
metrics,
checks the metadata quality and standards
compliance, helps
identify areas for improvement.
The proposed approach has five main areas of impact.
First, it supports creating AI-ready biodiverse dataset from
collection information. Second, it introduces
automated metadata extraction, reducing the
manual effort needed to structure historical catalog text.
Third, it connects
Darwin Core and Croissant, linking
biodiversity domain semantics with ML-oriented metadata.
Fourth, it includes FAIR metrics evaluation as a
part of workflow rather than treating FAIRness.
And fifth, the workflow can serve as a reference approach for
biodiversity collection that want to make
historical data more reusable in computational and
AI contexts.
To conclude, FAIR data provides a foundation for
trustworthy AI. AI LLMs can
structure historical catalog data while Darwin Core and
Croissant connect biodiversity standards with ML
workflows. FAIR metrics help evaluate AI readiness, and
this approach can be extended to other biodiversity collections.
Thanks
